newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian sugar stable as Ukraine VAT nears - trade.
newsitem.headline: Russian sugar stable as Ukraine VAT nears - trade.

text.p: MOSCOW, Sept 16 (Moscow) - Russian sugar prices will be stable in the short term, as Moscow introduces a 10 percent value-added tax on Ukrainian deliveries and mulls import quotas, traders and industry officials said on Monday.
"Right now, sugar prices are stable at $430-470 per tonne, and we expect them to be firm over the next few months," Mikhail Zharinov, head of marketing at Russian trader Alfa-Eko, said.
"Prices will not rise, because sugar imports in the first half of the year were too high."
Zharinov said larger imports in recent months, mostly from Ukraine, had given the Russian market reserves of over 300,000 tonnes of refined sugar.
"Ukraine has a margin to decrease its price, so it will continue to export," said one Western trader. "The new VAT will do nothing at all -- it's merely the nominal normalisation of the market."
He said the market was quiet as the summer's traditional preserve-making season had come to a close.

Russia said earlier this month that it would levy a 10 percent value-added tax on all Ukrainian raw and refined sugar imports from October 1 and that it planned possible quotas on all sugar imports to protect its own producers.
Zharinov said a number of Russian companies dealing in cheap Ukrainian sugar had already left the business on fears that the impending VAT would ruin their margins.

Ukraine exported around one million tonnes of sugar to Russia over the first six months of this year, a 30 percent increase on year-ago levels. Some traders said Ukrainian deliveries were already tapering off slightly.
Ukrainian officials and producers have called Russia's actions the start of a protectionist trade war, a charge Russians reject.

A senior official from Russia's Rossakhsvyokla sugar producers' association said the impending VAT was a positive and long-awaited measure, adding, "Ukranian sugar has pushed down prices on Russia's market, and our producers had to sell their own sugar at a loss."
Zharinov said Ukraine had been selling sugar to Russian buyers at around $400 per tonne, below average Russian costs of $480-500.

It is still unclear if or when Moscow will impose quotas on imports of white sugar, estimated by experts at 1.5 million tonnes a year. But Zharinov said this figure might include a quota of some 900,000 tonnes for Ukraine.
"In any case, we expect sugar prices to rise by some 10 percent only in January or February," he said.
